# How to use this guide

Pharmacology is a 75-hour second-year D.Pharm subject with 13 syllabus chapters. It is a "classification and facts" subject: most marks come from writing a clear **definition, classification, mechanism, uses, adverse effects and contraindications** for a drug group. Learn one unit every two or three days: read the notes, write each classification from memory, then answer the question bank without looking.

The guide follows the syllabus chapters one to one, except that **chapter 12 (chemotherapeutic agents, 12 hours) is split into two units** (12 and 13), so syllabus chapter 13 (biologicals) becomes guide unit 14.

| Guide unit | Syllabus chapter | Hours in syllabus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. General pharmacology | 1 | 10 |
| 2. Drugs acting on the peripheral nervous system | 2 | 11 |
| 3. Drugs acting on the eye | 3 | 2 |
| 4. Drugs acting on the central nervous system | 4 | 8 |
| 5. Drugs acting on the cardiovascular system | 5 | 6 |
| 6. Drugs acting on blood and blood-forming organs | 6 | 4 |
| 7. Drugs acting on the respiratory system | 7 | 2 |
| 8. Drugs acting on the gastrointestinal tract | 8 | 5 |
| 9. Drugs acting on the kidney | 9 | 2 |
| 10. Hormones and hormone antagonists | 10 | 8 |
| 11. Autocoids | 11 | 3 |
| 12. Chemotherapy I: principles and antibacterial drugs | 12 (first part) | 12 (shared) |
| 13. Chemotherapy II: antifungal, antiviral, antiprotozoal, anthelmintic and anticancer drugs | 12 (second part) | |
| 14. Biologicals | 13 | 2 |

Units 1, 2, 4, 5, 10 and 12–13 carry the most hours, so expect most long questions from them.

## Exam pattern (ER-2020 theory paper)

D.Pharm ER-2020 exams are yearly and are conducted by the state examining authority (in Himachal Pradesh, the HPTSB) under the PCI ER-2020 scheme. The theory paper is **80 marks, 3 hours**; another 20 marks come from sessional (internal) assessment. The usual paper looks like this. Confirm the exact split with your college, because boards sometimes change the format.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Objective questions (MCQs / one-word / fill in the blanks) – all compulsory | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| II | Short answers – attempt 10 of 11 | 10 × 3 = 30 |
| III | Long answers – attempt 6 of 7 | 6 × 5 = 30 |

In this guide the **long** questions are 5-mark answers and the **short** questions are 3-mark answers, to match this pattern. A few **very-short** (2-mark) questions are included for quick revision and for sessional tests. The full mock paper in the app follows the same pattern, and a 20-question quick MCQ test is there for daily practice.

## Probability ratings

- **High** – asked in most years; prepare the full answer with classification and a table.
- **Medium** – asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** – rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

Ratings are an estimate from the syllabus weight and the kind of questions usually set in D.Pharm papers. They are not a promise.

## Scoring tips for Pharmacology

1. **Use the standard answer frame** for any drug group: definition → classification (with 2–3 examples each) → mechanism of action → pharmacological actions → uses → adverse effects → contraindications → (dose only if you are sure). Examiners look for this order.
2. **Classification carries the most marks.** Write it as a neat tree or numbered list with headings (for example "A. Direct-acting – 1. Choline esters: …"). Learn at least two examples in every group.
3. **One line of mechanism** for every drug you name: "omeprazole irreversibly blocks H+/K+ ATPase", "warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase".
4. **Draw simple flow diagrams** where they help: synthesis of ACh and NA, arachidonic acid pathway, renin–angiotensin system, clotting cascade, nephron sites of diuretic action, malaria life cycle.
5. **Make comparison tables:** heparin vs warfarin, loop vs thiazide diuretics, depolarising vs non-depolarising blockers, first- vs second-generation antihistamines, TCAs vs SSRIs, typical vs atypical antipsychotics.
6. **Remember the "signature" facts** that MCQs love: antidotes (naloxone, flumazenil, protamine, vitamin K, atropine + pralidoxime, N-acetylcysteine, desferrioxamine), characteristic adverse effects (phenytoin – gum hypertrophy, ethambutol – optic neuritis, ACE inhibitor – dry cough, cyclophosphamide – haemorrhagic cystitis), and drugs of choice.
7. **Doses:** write a dose only when you are certain (for example paracetamol 500–1000 mg, maximum 4 g a day; adrenaline 0.5 mg IM of 1:1000 in anaphylaxis; albendazole 400 mg single dose). A wrong dose can cost marks.
8. **For a 5-mark answer** aim for about one and a half pages; **for a 3-mark answer** write 5–6 crisp points or a small table.
9. **Link to practice:** add one counselling point where it fits (take PPIs before breakfast, rinse mouth after steroid inhaler, complete the antibiotic course). It shows a pharmacist's understanding.
10. Revise the last-night revision sheet on the day before the exam, and attempt the full mock paper at least twice in 3 hours.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only a few hours, learn these topics with full classifications: **routes of administration and biotransformation**, **cholinergic and anticholinergic drugs (with OP poisoning)**, **adrenergic drugs and β-blockers**, **NSAIDs and paracetamol**, **antiepileptics and opioids**, **antihypertensives and antianginals**, **anticoagulants (heparin vs warfarin)**, **anti-ulcer drugs**, **diuretics**, **insulin and oral hypoglycaemics**, **corticosteroids**, **antihistamines**, **penicillins and anti-TB drugs**, **antimalarials**.

## General pharmacology (Unit 1)

| Topic | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| PK vs PD | ADME (body on drug) vs actions and mechanism (drug on body) |
| Fastest route / 100% bioavailability | IV |
| Avoid first-pass | Sublingual, transdermal, parenteral (partly rectal) |
| Bioavailability | AUC oral ÷ AUC IV × 100 |
| Phase I / Phase II | Oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis / conjugation (glucuronide commonest) |
| Enzyme inducers | Rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone |
| Enzyme inhibitors | Erythromycin, ketoconazole, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin |
| Alkaline urine | Removes weak acids (aspirin, phenobarbitone) |
| Steady state | About 4–5 half-lives |
| Agonist / antagonist | Affinity + intrinsic activity / affinity only |

## Autonomic drugs, LA and NSAIDs (Unit 2)

| Drug | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Neostigmine | Myasthenia gravis; reverses curare-like blockers |
| Physostigmine | Atropine poisoning; enters brain |
| OP poisoning | Atropine + pralidoxime (early) |
| Atropine | Tachycardia, dry mouth, mydriasis, cycloplegia; avoid in glaucoma, prostate enlargement |
| Adrenaline | Anaphylaxis 0.5 mg IM (1:1000) |
| Salbutamol | β2 agonist; tremor |
| Prazosin | First-dose hypotension |
| β-blockers | Contraindicated in asthma |
| Succinylcholine | Depolarising; hyperkalaemia; malignant hyperthermia → dantrolene |
| Local anaesthetics | Block Na+ channels; bupivacaine most cardiotoxic |
| Aspirin | Irreversible COX block; low dose antiplatelet; Reye's syndrome in children |
| Paracetamol | Max 4 g/day; overdose → N-acetylcysteine |

## Eye (Unit 3)

Miotic: pilocarpine. Mydriatic-cycloplegics: atropine (7–10 days) > homatropine > cyclopentolate > tropicamide (4–6 h). Phenylephrine: mydriasis without cycloplegia. Glaucoma: latanoprost, timolol, dorzolamide/acetazolamide, brimonidine, pilocarpine, mannitol. Mydriatics are contraindicated in angle-closure glaucoma.

## CNS (Unit 4)

| Drug | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Thiopentone | Ultra-short action by redistribution |
| Ketamine | Dissociative anaesthesia; raises BP |
| Benzodiazepines | ↑ frequency of GABA-A Cl− opening; antidote flumazenil |
| Status epilepticus | Lorazepam/diazepam IV |
| Absence seizures | Ethosuximide, valproate |
| Phenytoin / valproate | Gum hypertrophy / neural tube defects |
| SSRIs | First-line antidepressants; act after 2–4 weeks |
| MAOIs | Cheese reaction |
| Typical antipsychotics | Extrapyramidal effects; clozapine – agranulocytosis |
| Lithium | Narrow therapeutic range |
| Morphine | Respiratory depression, miosis, constipation; antidote naloxone |
| Alzheimer's | Donepezil, memantine |

## CVS (Unit 5)

| Drug | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| ACE inhibitors | Dry cough, angioedema, hyperkalaemia; not in pregnancy |
| Amlodipine | Ankle oedema |
| Pregnancy hypertension | Methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine |
| Hypertensive emergency | Sodium nitroprusside IV |
| GTN sublingual | Acts in 1–2 min; headache; never with sildenafil |
| Variant angina | Calcium channel blockers |
| PSVT | Adenosine |
| Amiodarone | Thyroid and lung toxicity |
| Statins | HMG-CoA reductase; myopathy |
| Digoxin | Na+/K+ ATPase; toxicity ↑ with low K+; antidote digoxin Fab |
| Shock | Anaphylactic – adrenaline; septic – noradrenaline; hypovolaemic – fluids |

## Blood (Unit 6)

| Item | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Iron | Absorbed as Fe2+; vitamin C helps; black stools; poisoning → desferrioxamine |
| B12 | Needs intrinsic factor; pernicious anaemia – injections |
| Folic acid | Prevents neural tube defects; not alone in B12 deficiency |
| Heparin | Immediate; aPTT; antidote protamine; safe in pregnancy |
| Warfarin | Oral; factors II, VII, IX, X; INR 2–3; antidote vitamin K; teratogenic |
| Clopidogrel | ADP (P2Y12) receptor block |
| Streptokinase / alteplase | Dissolve clots via plasmin; bleeding |
| Tranexamic acid | Antifibrinolytic |

## Respiratory, GIT and kidney (Units 7–9)

| Drug | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Salbutamol / salmeterol | Reliever / long-acting with inhaled steroid |
| Theophylline | PDE inhibitor; narrow therapeutic index |
| Inhaled steroids | Best controllers; rinse mouth |
| Montelukast | Leukotriene receptor block |
| Codeine, dextromethorphan | Dry cough only |
| Bromhexine, ambroxol, acetylcysteine | Mucolytics |
| Omeprazole | Blocks H+/K+ ATPase; before breakfast |
| H. pylori | PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin, 14 days |
| Ondansetron | 5-HT3 block; chemotherapy vomiting |
| Hyoscine | Motion sickness |
| Lactulose | Constipation, hepatic encephalopathy |
| ORS | 245 mOsm/L; glucose-coupled sodium absorption |
| Loperamide | Not in bloody diarrhoea or young children |
| Furosemide | Na+-K+-2Cl− (loop); pulmonary oedema; ototoxic |
| Thiazides | Na+-Cl− (DCT); hypertension; ↓ urinary Ca2+ |
| Spironolactone | Aldosterone antagonist; hyperkalaemia, gynaecomastia |
| Mannitol | Raised ICP; not in heart failure |
| Desmopressin | V2 agonist; central DI, bed-wetting |

## Hormones (Unit 10)

| Drug | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Levothyroxine | Hypothyroidism; empty stomach; TSH monitoring |
| Carbimazole | Blocks peroxidase; agranulocytosis |
| PTU | First trimester; thyroid storm |
| PTH / calcitonin | Raise / lower plasma calcium |
| Calcitriol | Active vitamin D; chronic kidney disease |
| Regular insulin | Standard IV insulin (ketoacidosis) |
| Metformin | First-line type 2; lactic acidosis (rare) |
| Glibenclamide | Hypoglycaemia |
| Oxytocin | Labour induction, PPH |
| Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg | Emergency contraception |
| Corticosteroids | Taper slowly; dexamethasone no mineralocorticoid effect |

## Autocoids (Unit 11)

Histamine from histidine (mast cells): H1 – bronchoconstriction, itching; H2 – acid. First-generation antihistamines sedate and are anticholinergic; cetirizine, fexofenadine are non-sedating. 5-HT from tryptophan (90% in gut); ondansetron blocks 5-HT3; sumatriptan (5-HT1B/1D agonist) for migraine. PGs from arachidonic acid (COX); misoprostol – NSAID ulcer; dinoprostone – labour; carboprost – PPH; alprostadil – patent ductus.

## Chemotherapy (Units 12–13)

| Drug | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Penicillins | Cell wall; anaphylaxis |
| Ceftriaxone | Meningitis, typhoid, gonorrhoea |
| Aminoglycosides | 30S; ototoxic, nephrotoxic; not oral |
| Fluoroquinolones | DNA gyrase; tendon rupture; not in children/pregnancy |
| Macrolides | 50S; penicillin alternative; atypical pneumonia |
| Tetracyclines | 30S; tooth staining; doxycycline for scrub typhus |
| Cotrimoxazole | Sequential folate block; Stevens–Johnson syndrome |
| TB regimen | 2HRZE + 4HRE |
| Isoniazid / rifampicin | Neuropathy (pyridoxine) / orange urine, enzyme inducer |
| Pyrazinamide / ethambutol | Hepatotoxic, gout / optic neuritis |
| Amphotericin B | Ergosterol binding; nephrotoxic |
| Fluconazole | Candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis |
| Acyclovir | Herpes, varicella |
| HIV first-line (India) | Tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir |
| Metronidazole | Amoebiasis, anaerobes; no alcohol |
| Albendazole | 400 mg single dose for common worms |
| Vivax malaria | Chloroquine + primaquine 14 days |
| Falciparum / severe | ACT / injectable artesunate |
| Cyclophosphamide | Haemorrhagic cystitis (mesna) |
| Methotrexate | DHFR; folinic acid rescue |
| Doxorubicin / bleomycin | Heart / lung toxicity |

## Biologicals (Unit 14)

Made from living cells; injected; cold chain 2–8 °C; biosimilars = similar, not identical. Live vaccines not in pregnancy. Equine sera → serum sickness. -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanised, -umab human, -cept fusion protein. Rituximab (CD20), trastuzumab (HER2), infliximab/adalimumab (TNF-α; screen for TB), omalizumab (IgE).

practicals.markdown:
# Introduction to experimental pharmacology

**Aim:** To understand the purpose, scope and rules of experimental pharmacology, and how the ER-2020 practicals are done using simulation software.

> Under ER-2020, animals are **not** used for any of the listed experiments. All experiments are carried out or demonstrated with software such as **Ex-Pharm** or other suitable simulation programs.

## Principle

**Experimental pharmacology** studies the effects of drugs on living systems (whole animals, isolated organs, tissues or cells) under controlled conditions, before and alongside studies in humans. It helps to:

1. Find new drugs and screen compounds for a wanted action (screening).
2. Work out the **mechanism of action** and the **dose–response** relationship.
3. Compare the potency and efficacy of drugs (bioassay).
4. Detect toxicity before a drug is given to humans (pre-clinical safety).
5. Teach students how drugs act.

### Ethics and the 3 Rs

In India animal experiments are regulated by the **Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA**, earlier CPCSEA) under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960. Every institution using animals needs an **Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC)**. The guiding principle is the **3 Rs**:

| R | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Replacement** | Use non-animal methods wherever possible | Computer simulation, cell culture, isolated tissues from slaughterhouses |
| **Reduction** | Use the fewest animals that give a valid result | Good experimental design and statistics |
| **Refinement** | Reduce pain and distress | Anaesthesia, humane end points, good housing |

ER-2020 practicals apply **Replacement** fully by using software.

## Requirements

Computer with simulation software (Ex-Pharm or similar), practical record book, graph paper or spreadsheet.

## Procedure

1. Open the software and read the introduction screen for the experiment.
2. Note the animal or tissue being simulated, the apparatus and the drugs available.
3. Record the **control (baseline) reading** before giving any drug.
4. Select a drug and dose, "administer" it by the route shown and record the response at the stated times.
5. Repeat with a standard drug and with the test drug; compare with control.
6. Tabulate results, draw graphs (dose–response curves) and write conclusions.

## Observations

| Group | Drug and dose | Response before | Response after | Change (%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control | Vehicle (saline) | | | |
| Standard | | | | |
| Test | | | | |

```text
 % change = (Response after − Response before) ÷ Response before × 100
```

## Result

The aims, scope, ethical regulation and simulated methods of experimental pharmacology were studied.

## Precautions

1. Always record a control reading first.
2. Use the dose units shown in the software (mg/kg) and note the route.
3. Do not change more than one variable at a time.

## Viva questions

1. **What is experimental pharmacology?** The study of drug effects on animals, isolated tissues or cells under controlled conditions.
2. **What are the 3 Rs?** Replacement, Reduction and Refinement of animal use.
3. **Which body regulates animal experiments in India?** CCSEA (formerly CPCSEA); each institution has an IAEC.
4. **Why does ER-2020 use software?** To avoid using animals (replacement) while still teaching drug effects.
5. **What is a bioassay?** Measuring the potency of a drug by comparing its biological effect with that of a standard.
practicals.title: Introduction to experimental pharmacology

practicals.markdown:
# Study of laboratory animals: mice, rats, guinea pigs and rabbits

**Aim:** To study the common laboratory animals, their features, handling, housing and uses in experimental pharmacology.

> This is a theory-and-record exercise. Live animals are not used under ER-2020; use pictures, charts and the simulation software.

## Principle

The choice of animal depends on the response being studied, size, cost, ease of handling, breeding time and how closely the animal's response resembles humans. Animals must be healthy, of known strain, age, sex and weight, and kept under standard conditions (about 22 ± 3 °C, 12-hour light/dark cycle, clean cages, food and water freely available).

## Requirements

Charts or software images of animals, practical record book.

## Procedure

1. Study the scientific name, strain, features and uses of each animal (table below).
2. Learn the correct method of holding each animal (from charts or video).
3. Note the common routes used in each and the uses in screening.
4. Record the information in the practical book.

## Observations

| Animal | Common strains | Key features | Main uses in pharmacology |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Mouse** (*Mus musculus*) | Swiss albino, BALB/c | Small (about 20–30 g), cheap, breeds fast, needs little drug | Screening of CNS drugs (actophotometer, rota-rod), analgesics (writhing, hot plate), anticonvulsants, acute toxicity (LD50), chemotherapy |
| **Rat** (*Rattus norvegicus*) | Wistar, Sprague–Dawley | Medium size (about 150–250 g), no vomiting reflex, no gall bladder | Anti-inflammatory (paw oedema), anticonvulsant (MES), antiulcer, antidiabetic, toxicity studies, isolated organs (uterus, ileum) |
| **Guinea pig** (*Cavia porcellus*) | Dunkin–Hartley | Very sensitive to histamine; needs dietary vitamin C | Antihistamine and anti-asthma screening, isolated ileum (histamine, ACh), anaphylaxis, local anaesthetics (wheal test) |
| **Rabbit** (*Oryctolagus cuniculus*) | New Zealand white | Large ear veins, large eyes, stable body temperature | **Pyrogen test**, eye studies (mydriatics, miotics, local anaesthetics), skin and eye irritation tests, antibody production |

### Handling (summary)

- **Mouse:** lift by the base of the tail; hold the loose skin behind the neck between thumb and finger for injection.
- **Rat:** hold round the shoulders/chest with the thumb under the jaw; or by the scruff.
- **Guinea pig:** support the hind quarters with one hand and hold the chest with the other.
- **Rabbit:** never lift by the ears; hold the scruff and support the hind quarters; use a rabbit holder (restrainer) for ear-vein work.

## Result

The features, handling and pharmacological uses of mice, rats, guinea pigs and rabbits were studied.

## Precautions

1. Handle animals gently to avoid stress (stress changes results).
2. Use animals of the same sex, age and weight in a group.
3. Wear gloves and lab coat; wash hands after handling.

## Viva questions

1. **Which animal is used for the pyrogen test?** Rabbit.
2. **Why is the guinea pig used for antihistamine studies?** It is very sensitive to histamine.
3. **Which common laboratory animal cannot vomit?** The rat.
4. **Which strain of rat is common in Indian labs?** Wistar albino rats.
5. **Why should a rabbit not be lifted by the ears?** It causes pain and injury; support the scruff and hind quarters.
practicals.title: Study of laboratory animals: mice, rats, guinea pigs and rabbits

practicals.markdown:
# Commonly used instruments in experimental pharmacology

**Aim:** To study the instruments used in experimental pharmacology, their principle and uses.

> Study the instruments from the laboratory, charts or the simulation software. No animals are used.

## Principle

Each instrument measures a particular drug response in a standard, repeatable way: movement, muscle coordination, pain reaction, convulsions, or the contraction of an isolated tissue.

## Requirements

Instruments or their images, simulation software, practical record book.

## Procedure

1. Identify each instrument and draw a labelled sketch.
2. Write its principle, main parts and use.
3. In the software, note how each instrument records a response.

## Observations

| Instrument | Principle / parts | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Actophotometer** | Square or round arena with light beams falling on photocells; each beam cut by the animal is counted | Locomotor activity – CNS stimulants (↑ count) and depressants (↓ count) |
| **Rota-rod** | Rod rotating at a set speed; animal must keep its balance; fall-off time recorded | Muscle relaxant and motor coordination (diazepam reduces time on rod) |
| **Analgesiometer** – Eddy's hot plate | Plate kept at a constant temperature; time to paw licking or jumping | Centrally acting analgesics (morphine) |
| **Analgesiometer** – tail-flick (radiant heat) | Heated wire under the tail; time to flick the tail | Centrally acting analgesics |
| **Electroconvulsiometer** | Delivers a measured electric current (mA) for a short time through ear or corneal electrodes | Maximal electroshock seizures – screening of antiepileptics |
| **Elevated plus maze** | Plus-shaped platform raised above the floor: two open and two closed arms | Anxiolytic drugs (↑ time in open arms) |
| **Organ bath** with kymograph or transducer | Tissue in a warmed, aerated physiological salt solution; contractions recorded | Isolated ileum, uterus, heart – dose–response curves, bioassay |
| **Student's organ bath / Dale's bath** | Inner bath for tissue, outer water jacket with thermostat | Isolated tissue experiments |
| **Sherrington rotating drum (kymograph)** | Smoked paper on a rotating drum; lever writes the response | Recording contractions (older method) |
| **Plethysmometer** | Measures paw volume by fluid displacement | Anti-inflammatory activity (paw oedema) |
| **Inclined plane** | Board tilted at a set angle; animal must stay on it | Muscle relaxants, sedatives |
| **Cook's pole-climbing apparatus** | Animal learns to climb a pole to avoid a shock after a sound signal (conditioned avoidance) | Antipsychotics |

## Result

The principle and uses of common instruments in experimental pharmacology were studied.

## Precautions

1. Calibrate instruments (temperature, current, rpm) before use.
2. Keep the testing room quiet and at constant light and temperature.
3. Electroconvulsiometer: handle electrodes carefully.

## Viva questions

1. **What does an actophotometer measure?** Locomotor activity, using photocells.
2. **Which instrument screens muscle relaxants?** Rota-rod.
3. **Name two analgesiometers.** Eddy's hot plate and tail-flick (radiant heat) apparatus.
4. **What is an organ bath used for?** To keep an isolated tissue alive in warm, aerated salt solution and record its responses to drugs.
5. **What does a plethysmometer measure?** Volume of the rat paw (for anti-inflammatory studies).
practicals.title: Commonly used instruments in experimental pharmacology

practicals.markdown:
# Routes of drug administration in animals

**Aim:** To study the different routes of drug administration in laboratory animals and the volumes and needles normally used.

> Learn the techniques from charts, videos and the simulation software. Animals are not used under ER-2020.

## Principle

The route decides the speed and extent of absorption. In experiments the dose is given as **mg per kg body weight**, so the volume injected depends on the weight of the animal. Small rodents cannot take large volumes, and some routes (IV in mice) need skill.

## Requirements

Charts or software, syringes (1 ml tuberculin and 2–5 ml), needles of different gauges, oral feeding needle (gavage cannula), animal holders, practical record book.

## Procedure

1. Study each route, the site and the restraint used (table below).
2. Calculate the dose volume for a given animal weight (calculation section).
3. Record in the practical book.

## Observations

| Route | Abbreviation | Site / method | Animals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Oral** (per oral) | p.o. | Oral feeding needle (blunt, ball-tipped) passed into the stomach | Mice, rats |
| **Intraperitoneal** | i.p. | Lower abdomen, to one side of the midline, needle at an angle (avoids bladder and gut) | Mice, rats – most common in screening |
| **Subcutaneous** | s.c. | Loose skin at the back of the neck or flank | All |
| **Intramuscular** | i.m. | Thigh muscles | Rats, rabbits |
| **Intravenous** | i.v. | **Tail vein** (mice, rats – warm the tail first to dilate the vein); **marginal ear vein** (rabbits) | All |
| Intradermal | i.d. | Into the skin layers (raises a bleb) | Guinea pigs, rabbits |
| Intracerebroventricular | i.c.v. | Into brain ventricles (specialised) | Rats, mice |
| Topical / instillation | — | Eye drops into the conjunctival sac | Rabbits |
| Inhalation | — | Volatile anaesthetics in a chamber | All |

## Calculation

```text
 Dose to inject (mg) = Dose (mg/kg) × Body weight (kg)
 Volume to inject (ml) = Dose to inject (mg) ÷ Concentration of solution (mg/ml)

 Example: diazepam 4 mg/kg for a 25 g mouse, solution 0.4 mg/ml
   Dose = 4 × 0.025 = 0.1 mg
   Volume = 0.1 ÷ 0.4 = 0.25 ml
```

Keep the volumes small for small animals (for example about 10 ml/kg orally or i.p. in mice is commonly used in screening).

## Result

The routes of drug administration in laboratory animals and dose calculations were studied.

## Precautions

1. Use the smallest needle that does the job; use a fresh sterile needle for each animal.
2. Remove air bubbles before IV injection.
3. Pull back slightly before i.p. injection to make sure the needle is not in the gut or a vessel.
4. Restrain properly to avoid injury to the animal and the handler.

## Viva questions

1. **Which vein is used for IV injection in rabbits?** The marginal ear vein.
2. **Which vein is used in mice and rats?** The lateral tail vein.
3. **Why is the i.p. route popular in screening?** It is easy, quick and gives fairly fast absorption.
4. **What is a gavage (feeding) needle?** A blunt, ball-tipped needle for giving drugs directly into the stomach.
5. **How is dose expressed in animal experiments?** In mg per kg body weight.
practicals.title: Routes of drug administration in animals

practicals.markdown:
# Types of pre-clinical experiments: in vivo, in vitro, ex vivo

**Aim:** To study the different types of pre-clinical experiments used in drug research and their merits and limitations.

## Principle

Before a new drug is tested in humans (clinical trials), its activity and safety are studied in **pre-clinical** experiments. These are classified by where the experiment is done.

## Requirements

Charts, simulation software, practical record book.

## Procedure

1. Study the definition and examples of each type (table).
2. Note the place of pre-clinical studies in new drug development.
3. Record in the practical book.

## Observations

| Type | Meaning | Examples | Merits | Limitations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **In vivo** ("in the living") | Experiment on a whole living animal | Analgesic test on mice, anticonvulsant test in rats, pyrogen test in rabbits, toxicity studies | Shows the effect in a whole body with absorption, metabolism and excretion | Uses animals, costly, variable, ethical issues |
| **In vitro** ("in glass") | Experiment outside a living organism on cells, enzymes, receptors or microbes | Enzyme inhibition assays, cell culture, receptor binding, MIC testing of antibiotics | Fast, cheap, no animal use, good for mechanism | Does not show whole-body effects |
| **Ex vivo** ("out of the living") | Tissue taken from an organism is studied outside the body, often after the animal was given the drug | Isolated organ studies (ileum, heart, aorta), tissue taken from treated animals | Closer to real tissue than cells; controlled conditions | Tissue survives only for hours; nerve and hormonal links lost |
| **In silico** | Computer modelling and simulation | Molecular docking, Ex-Pharm simulations | No animals, very cheap | Only as good as the model |
| In situ | Organ studied in its normal place in an anaesthetised animal | Blood pressure recording in an anaesthetised animal | Natural blood supply | Needs anaesthesia and skill |

### Place in new drug development

```text
 Drug discovery → Pre-clinical studies (in silico, in vitro, ex vivo, in vivo:
   pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, acute/sub-acute/chronic toxicity,
   mutagenicity, carcinogenicity, teratogenicity)
 → Clinical trial phases I, II, III → Approval (in India, CDSCO / DCGI
   under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019) → Phase IV (post-marketing)
```

## Result

In vivo, in vitro, ex vivo, in situ and in silico experiments and their roles in pre-clinical drug development were studied.

## Precautions

1. Always include control groups.
2. Results from one model should be confirmed in another before conclusions are drawn.

## Viva questions

1. **What is an in vitro study?** An experiment done outside a living organism, e.g. on cells or enzymes.
2. **Give an example of an ex vivo study.** Isolated frog heart or guinea pig ileum in an organ bath.
3. **What is in silico?** Computer-based modelling or simulation.
4. **Why are pre-clinical studies needed?** To show activity and safety before giving a drug to humans.
5. **Who approves clinical trials in India?** The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (DCGI).
practicals.title: Types of pre-clinical experiments: in vivo, in vitro, ex vivo

practicals.markdown:
# Techniques of blood collection from animals

**Aim:** To study the methods used to collect blood from laboratory animals for pharmacological and toxicological studies.

> Learn from charts, videos and software. No animals are used under ER-2020.

## Principle

Blood samples are needed to measure drug levels (pharmacokinetics), blood sugar, cholesterol, liver and kidney function, and blood counts. The method depends on the species, the volume needed, how often samples are taken and whether the animal is to survive. The total volume taken must be limited to protect the animal's health, as laid down in ethics guidelines.

## Requirements

Charts or software, capillary tubes, syringes and fine needles, collection tubes with anticoagulant (EDTA, heparin, citrate) or plain tubes for serum, local anaesthetic, warming lamp, cotton, practical record book.

## Procedure

1. Study each method, its site, the volume obtained and the animals in which it is used (table).
2. Note the anticoagulant needed for each test.
3. Record in the practical book.

## Observations

| Method | Site and technique | Animals | Remarks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Retro-orbital (orbital sinus) puncture** | Fine capillary tube inserted at the inner corner of the eye into the venous sinus, under anaesthesia | Mice, rats | Small to moderate volume; skill needed; repeated sampling possible but now discouraged |
| **Tail vein / tail tip** | Tail warmed to dilate vein; needle prick or small snip of tail tip | Mice, rats | Small volumes, e.g. blood glucose |
| **Saphenous vein** | Hind leg vein pricked after shaving | Mice, rats, guinea pigs | Repeated small samples, little stress |
| **Marginal ear vein / central ear artery** | Vein dilated by warming or xylene rubbing; needle or small cut | Rabbits | Common method in rabbits |
| **Cardiac puncture** | Needle through the chest wall into the heart under deep anaesthesia | Mice, rats, guinea pigs, rabbits | Large volume; **terminal** procedure only |
| **Jugular vein** | Under anaesthesia, sometimes by a catheter | Rats, rabbits | Repeated sampling with cannula |
| Decapitation / terminal bleeding | At end of study under ethics approval | Rodents | Terminal |

### Choice of tube

| Test | Tube |
| --- | --- |
| Blood counts | EDTA |
| Plasma drug levels | Heparin or EDTA |
| Clotting tests | Sodium citrate |
| Serum chemistry (liver, kidney tests) | Plain tube (allow to clot) |

## Result

The common methods of blood collection from laboratory animals were studied.

## Precautions

1. Use anaesthesia where required; terminal methods only under approval.
2. Do not exceed the permitted blood volume.
3. Use sterile equipment and apply pressure to stop bleeding.
4. Label tubes with animal number, time and group.

## Viva questions

1. **Which method gives the largest volume of blood?** Cardiac puncture (terminal).
2. **Which method is used in rabbits?** Marginal ear vein (or central ear artery).
3. **What is retro-orbital puncture?** Collection from the orbital venous sinus behind the eye with a capillary tube.
4. **Which anticoagulant is used for blood counts?** EDTA.
5. **Why is the tail warmed before sampling?** To dilate the tail vein.
practicals.title: Techniques of blood collection from animals

practicals.markdown:
# Effect of local anaesthetics on the rabbit eye

**Aim:** To study the surface (topical) local anaesthetic effect of drugs on the rabbit cornea using simulation software (Ex-Pharm or similar).

## Principle

Touching the cornea normally causes an immediate blink – the **corneal reflex**. A **local anaesthetic** applied to the cornea blocks sodium channels in the sensory nerve endings, so touching the cornea no longer produces a blink. The **onset**, **intensity** (number of touches without a blink) and **duration** of anaesthesia are compared for different drugs. Surface anaesthetics such as lidocaine (lignocaine) and tetracaine produce this effect; procaine penetrates mucous membranes poorly and is a weak surface anaesthetic.

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: rabbit in a holder, test drugs (lidocaine 2–4% solution, tetracaine/amethocaine drops, procaine solution, normal saline as control), dropper, a fine hair or bristle (for touching the cornea), stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Select the rabbit and check the corneal reflex in both eyes by touching the cornea gently with the bristle (the animal blinks).
2. Instil the control (saline) into one eye and the test local anaesthetic into the other, holding the lower lid like a cup; close the lids for a minute.
3. Test the corneal reflex every few minutes (e.g. every 5 minutes): touch the cornea a fixed number of times (e.g. 10 touches) and count the blinks.
4. Record the time of onset (no blink), the time of complete anaesthesia and the time when the reflex returns.
5. Repeat with other local anaesthetics and compare.

## Observations

| Time (min) | Saline eye: blinks / 10 touches | Lidocaine eye: blinks / 10 touches | Procaine eye: blinks / 10 touches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 (before) | 10 | 10 | 10 |
| 5 | | | |
| 10 | | | |
| 20 | | | |
| 30 | | | |
| 45 | | | |

```text
 Onset of anaesthesia   = time when the blink first fails
 Duration of anaesthesia = time of return of reflex − time of onset
```

## Result

The local anaesthetic (lidocaine) abolished the corneal reflex with an onset of ___ min and a duration of ___ min; saline had no effect. (Fill in from your simulation.)

## Precautions

1. Touch the cornea gently and from the side, not the front, so the animal does not see the bristle.
2. Do not touch the eyelashes or lid margins.
3. Use the same number of touches each time.
4. Keep one eye as control.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the corneal reflex?** Blinking when the cornea is touched.
2. **How do local anaesthetics act?** By blocking voltage-gated sodium channels in nerves.
3. **Why is procaine a poor surface anaesthetic?** It does not penetrate mucous membranes well.
4. **Name two surface anaesthetics used in the eye.** Lidocaine and tetracaine (proparacaine is also used).
5. **Why should a patient avoid rubbing the eye after topical anaesthesia?** The cornea is insensitive and may be injured.
practicals.title: Effect of local anaesthetics on the rabbit eye

practicals.markdown:
# Mydriatic effect on the rabbit eye

**Aim:** To study the effect of mydriatic drugs on pupil size and light reflex in the rabbit eye using simulation software.

## Principle

Pupil size depends on two muscles of the iris: the **sphincter pupillae** (parasympathetic, M3 – miosis) and the **dilator pupillae** (sympathetic, α1 – mydriasis).

- **Anticholinergics** (atropine, homatropine, tropicamide) block M3 receptors → mydriasis, **loss of light reflex** and cycloplegia.
- **Sympathomimetics** (phenylephrine, adrenaline, ephedrine) stimulate α1 receptors of the dilator → mydriasis with the **light reflex kept**.

The pupil diameter is measured before and at intervals after instilling the drug, and the light reflex is tested.

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: rabbit in a holder, atropine sulphate 1% eye drops, phenylephrine eye drops, normal saline, measuring scale (mm), torch, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Measure the pupil diameter of both eyes in diffuse light and test the light reflex with a torch.
2. Instil saline into one eye (control) and the mydriatic into the other.
3. Measure pupil diameter and test the light reflex at fixed intervals (e.g. 5, 10, 20, 30 minutes).
4. Repeat with a sympathomimetic mydriatic and compare.

## Observations

| Time (min) | Control eye pupil (mm) | Light reflex | Atropine eye pupil (mm) | Light reflex | Phenylephrine eye pupil (mm) | Light reflex |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | | + | | + | | + |
| 10 | | | | | | |
| 20 | | | | | | |
| 30 | | | | | | |

```text
 Increase in pupil size (mm) = Pupil diameter after drug − Pupil diameter before
```

## Result

Atropine produced mydriasis with loss of light reflex; phenylephrine produced mydriasis with the light reflex present; saline had no effect.

## Precautions

1. Measure the pupil under the same lighting each time.
2. Instil the same number of drops each time and keep the other eye as control.
3. Avoid touching the cornea with the dropper.

## Viva questions

1. **What is a mydriatic?** A drug that dilates the pupil.
2. **Why is the light reflex lost with atropine but not with phenylephrine?** Atropine paralyses the sphincter pupillae; phenylephrine only contracts the dilator, so the sphincter still responds to light.
3. **Which mydriatic is shortest acting?** Tropicamide.
4. **When are mydriatics contraindicated?** Angle-closure glaucoma.
5. **What is cycloplegia?** Paralysis of accommodation.
practicals.title: Mydriatic effect on the rabbit eye

practicals.markdown:
# Miotic effect on the rabbit eye

**Aim:** To study the effect of miotic drugs on pupil size and light reflex of the rabbit eye using simulation software.

## Principle

**Miotics** constrict the pupil by contracting the sphincter pupillae (M3 receptors). Direct cholinergic agonists (pilocarpine, carbachol) act on the receptor; anticholinesterases (physostigmine) prevent breakdown of acetylcholine. A miotic can also reverse the mydriasis produced by a sympathomimetic, while the mydriasis of atropine (a receptor blocker) is resisted by pilocarpine because the receptors are blocked.

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: rabbit in a holder, pilocarpine nitrate 1% (or physostigmine) eye drops, normal saline, measuring scale (mm), torch, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Measure the pupil diameter of both eyes and test the light reflex.
2. Instil saline (control) into one eye and the miotic into the other.
3. Record pupil diameter and light reflex at fixed intervals (e.g. 5, 10, 20, 30 minutes).
4. Optional: instil a miotic into an eye previously dilated with phenylephrine and observe reversal.

## Observations

| Time (min) | Control eye pupil (mm) | Light reflex | Pilocarpine eye pupil (mm) | Light reflex |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | | + | | + |
| 10 | | | | |
| 20 | | | | |
| 30 | | | | |

```text
 Decrease in pupil size (mm) = Pupil diameter before − Pupil diameter after drug
```

## Result

Pilocarpine produced miosis (decrease of ___ mm at ___ min); saline produced no change.

## Precautions

1. Keep lighting constant during measurements.
2. Use the other eye as control.
3. Do not let the dropper touch the eye.

## Viva questions

1. **What is a miotic?** A drug that constricts the pupil.
2. **Mechanism of pilocarpine?** Direct muscarinic (M3) agonist on the sphincter pupillae.
3. **Clinical use of miotics?** Glaucoma (especially acute angle-closure), reversal of mydriasis.
4. **How does physostigmine produce miosis?** By inhibiting cholinesterase, so ACh accumulates.
5. **Which systemic drug causes pin-point pupils?** Morphine (opioids).
practicals.title: Miotic effect on the rabbit eye

practicals.markdown:
# Effect of analgesics using an analgesiometer

**Aim:** To study the analgesic effect of a drug (for example morphine or pentazocine) in mice or rats using the **Eddy's hot plate** or **tail-flick (radiant heat) analgesiometer**, by simulation.

## Principle

Thermal pain tests measure the **reaction time** of an animal to a heat stimulus. **Centrally acting analgesics** (opioids such as morphine, pentazocine, tramadol) raise the pain threshold, so the reaction time increases. Peripherally acting NSAIDs act poorly in these tests.

- **Hot plate (Eddy's):** the animal is placed on a plate kept at a constant temperature (commonly about 55 °C); the time until it licks its paw or jumps is the reaction time.
- **Tail-flick:** a heated wire (radiant heat) under the tail; the time until the tail is flicked away is recorded.

A **cut-off time** (for example 15 seconds on the hot plate, 10–12 seconds for tail-flick) is fixed so the tissue is not injured.

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: mice or rats, hot plate or tail-flick analgesiometer, morphine (standard), test drug, saline, syringes, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Divide the animals into groups: control (saline), standard (morphine) and test.
2. Record the **basal reaction time** of each animal (mean of two or three readings).
3. Give the drug by the route shown (s.c. or i.p.).
4. Record the reaction time at intervals (e.g. 15, 30, 60, 90 minutes), stopping at the cut-off time.
5. Calculate the increase in reaction time and the percentage analgesia.

## Observations

| Group | Basal reaction time (s) | 15 min | 30 min | 60 min | 90 min |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control (saline) | | | | | |
| Morphine | | | | | |
| Test drug | | | | | |

```text
 % analgesia (maximum possible effect) =
       (Test reaction time − Basal reaction time)
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────── × 100
       (Cut-off time − Basal reaction time)
```

## Result

Morphine increased the reaction time significantly compared with control, showing central analgesic activity; peak effect at ___ min.

## Precautions

1. Keep the plate temperature constant and check it before each test.
2. Never exceed the cut-off time.
3. Use animals of similar weight and sex; acclimatise them to the room.
4. Record readings at exact times.

## Viva questions

1. **Which analgesics are detected by the hot plate test?** Centrally acting analgesics such as opioids.
2. **Why is a cut-off time used?** To prevent tissue damage.
3. **What is the reaction time?** Time between applying the heat stimulus and the animal's response (paw licking, jumping or tail flick).
4. **Which receptor does morphine act on?** Mainly µ opioid receptors.
5. **Which test is used for peripheral analgesics?** Acetic acid writhing test.
practicals.title: Effect of analgesics using an analgesiometer

practicals.markdown:
# Analgesic activity by the acetic acid writhing test

**Aim:** To study the analgesic activity of a drug (for example aspirin or diclofenac) by the acetic acid-induced writhing test in mice, by simulation.

## Principle

Intraperitoneal injection of a dilute **acetic acid** solution (commonly 0.6% v/v, 10 ml/kg) irritates the peritoneum and causes release of prostaglandins and other pain mediators. The mouse shows **writhing**: stretching of the body, contraction of the abdominal muscles and extension of the hind limbs. **Peripherally acting analgesics (NSAIDs)** that inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, and also opioids, reduce the number of writhes. The test is sensitive and simple, but not specific.

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: mice, 0.6% acetic acid, aspirin or diclofenac (standard), test drug, saline, syringes, observation boxes, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Divide mice into control, standard and test groups.
2. Give saline, standard or test drug (orally or i.p.) and wait for the absorption time shown (e.g. 30 minutes for i.p., longer for oral).
3. Inject acetic acid i.p.
4. After a short latent period (about 5 minutes), count the number of writhes for a fixed period (e.g. 10 or 15 minutes).
5. Calculate the percentage inhibition of writhing.

## Observations

| Group | Drug and dose | Number of writhes (mean) | % inhibition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control | Saline | | — |
| Standard | Aspirin / diclofenac | | |
| Test | | | |

```text
 % inhibition = (Mean writhes in control − Mean writhes in treated) ÷ Mean writhes in control × 100
```

## Result

The standard drug reduced the number of writhes by ___%, showing peripheral analgesic activity.

## Precautions

1. Use freshly prepared acetic acid of the correct strength.
2. Count writhes for exactly the same time in all groups.
3. Inject i.p. in the lower abdomen to avoid puncturing the gut.

## Viva questions

1. **What is writhing?** Abdominal contraction with body stretching and hind-limb extension due to peritoneal pain.
2. **Which mediators are involved?** Prostaglandins, bradykinin and others.
3. **Which drugs are detected by this test?** Peripheral analgesics (NSAIDs) and also central analgesics.
4. **What is the standard drug?** Aspirin or diclofenac (morphine for central analgesics).
5. **Why is a latent period allowed?** Writhing starts a few minutes after the acetic acid injection.
practicals.title: Analgesic activity by the acetic acid writhing test

practicals.markdown:
# Screening of anticonvulsants using an electroconvulsiometer

**Aim:** To study the anticonvulsant effect of a drug (for example phenytoin) against **maximal electroshock (MES)** seizures in rats, by simulation.

## Principle

A strong electric current passed briefly through the brain (by ear or corneal electrodes) produces a **maximal seizure** with typical phases. The **tonic hind-limb extension (THLE)** phase is abolished or shortened by drugs effective in **generalised tonic–clonic (grand mal) epilepsy**, such as phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone and valproate. Commonly used settings are about **150 mA for 0.2 s in rats** (lower current, about 50 mA, in mice).

```text
 Phases of MES seizure:
 1. Tonic flexion → 2. Tonic extension (hind limbs stretched backwards) →
 3. Clonic convulsions → 4. Stupor → 5. Recovery (or death)
```

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: rats, electroconvulsiometer with ear (or corneal) electrodes, phenytoin (standard), test drug, saline, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Divide rats into control, standard and test groups.
2. Apply the current to the control animal and note the duration of each phase, especially **tonic hind-limb extension**.
3. Give phenytoin (or test drug) by the route shown; wait for the time of peak effect.
4. Apply the same current again and record the duration of each phase.
5. Note whether THLE is abolished or reduced and whether the animal recovers.

## Observations

| Group | Flexion (s) | Extension (s) | Clonus (s) | Stupor (s) | Recovery / death |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control | | | | | |
| Phenytoin | | | | | |
| Test drug | | | | | |

```text
 % protection = (Number of animals without THLE ÷ Total animals in group) × 100
 or % reduction in THLE = (Control THLE − Treated THLE) ÷ Control THLE × 100
```

## Result

Phenytoin abolished/reduced the tonic hind-limb extension phase, showing anticonvulsant activity against generalised tonic–clonic seizures.

## Precautions

1. Use the same current strength and duration in all animals.
2. Moisten electrodes with saline for good contact.
3. Test at the time of peak drug effect.
4. Handle the electrodes carefully.

## Viva questions

1. **Which phase is used to judge anticonvulsant activity in MES?** Tonic hind-limb extension.
2. **The MES test is a model of which type of epilepsy?** Generalised tonic–clonic (grand mal).
3. **Which test is a model of absence seizures?** Pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)-induced seizures; ethosuximide protects.
4. **Name a standard drug for MES.** Phenytoin.
5. **Mechanism of phenytoin?** Prolongs the inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels.
practicals.title: Screening of anticonvulsants using an electroconvulsiometer

practicals.markdown:
# Screening of muscle relaxants using the rota-rod apparatus

**Aim:** To study the muscle relaxant (motor coordination-impairing) effect of a drug such as diazepam in mice using the rota-rod apparatus, by simulation.

## Principle

The rota-rod is a horizontal rod (with a rough surface) that rotates at a constant speed (commonly 20–25 rpm). A normal mouse can keep its balance on it for a long time. A **centrally acting muscle relaxant** or sedative (diazepam, baclofen) reduces muscle tone and coordination, so the mouse **falls off sooner**. The **fall-off time** is a measure of muscle relaxant activity.

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: mice, rota-rod apparatus, diazepam (standard), test drug, saline, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Train the mice on the rotating rod; select those that stay on for a set time (e.g. 3–5 minutes) in a trial.
2. Record the basal fall-off time of each mouse.
3. Give saline, diazepam or test drug by the route shown.
4. Place each mouse on the rod at fixed intervals (e.g. 30, 60, 90 minutes) and record the fall-off time.
5. Calculate the percentage decrease in fall-off time.

## Observations

| Group | Basal fall-off time (s) | 30 min | 60 min | 90 min |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control | | | | |
| Diazepam | | | | |
| Test drug | | | | |

```text
 % decrease in fall-off time = (Basal time − Time after drug) ÷ Basal time × 100
```

## Result

Diazepam decreased the fall-off time by ___%, showing muscle relaxant activity.

## Precautions

1. Use only mice that pass the training trial.
2. Keep the rod speed constant.
3. Place mice gently in the same way each time.
4. Avoid noise and distraction in the room.

## Viva questions

1. **What does the rota-rod test measure?** Motor coordination and muscle relaxant activity.
2. **What is the standard drug?** Diazepam.
3. **How do benzodiazepines relax muscles?** By enhancing GABA-A-mediated inhibition in the spinal cord and brain.
4. **Name two centrally acting muscle relaxants.** Baclofen and tizanidine.
5. **Why are mice trained before the test?** To select animals that can normally stay on the rod, so results are reliable.
practicals.title: Screening of muscle relaxants using the rota-rod apparatus

practicals.markdown:
# Screening of CNS stimulants and depressants using an actophotometer

**Aim:** To study the effect of a CNS stimulant (caffeine or amphetamine) and a CNS depressant (diazepam or chlorpromazine) on the locomotor activity of mice using an actophotometer, by simulation.

## Principle

**Locomotor activity** is an index of alertness. In an actophotometer, beams of light fall on **photocells**; each time the animal moves across a beam, the beam is cut and a count is recorded on a digital counter. **CNS stimulants** increase the count; **CNS depressants** (sedatives, anxiolytics, antipsychotics) decrease it.

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: mice, actophotometer, caffeine (stimulant), diazepam or chlorpromazine (depressant), saline, syringes, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Switch on the actophotometer and check that the counter works.
2. Place each mouse in the arena for a fixed time (e.g. 10 minutes) and record the **basal activity score**.
3. Give saline, the stimulant or the depressant by the route shown.
4. After the absorption time (e.g. 30 minutes), place the mouse again for the same period and record the activity score.
5. Calculate the percentage change in activity.

## Observations

| Group | Basal count (10 min) | Count after drug (10 min) | % change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control | | | |
| Caffeine | | | |
| Diazepam | | | |

```text
 % change in activity = (Count after drug − Basal count) ÷ Basal count × 100
   (positive = stimulation; negative = depression)
```

## Result

Caffeine increased and diazepam decreased the locomotor activity, showing CNS stimulant and depressant effects respectively.

## Precautions

1. Test in a quiet room with constant light.
2. Observe each mouse for exactly the same time.
3. Clean the arena between animals (odours affect behaviour).

## Viva questions

1. **What does an actophotometer measure?** Locomotor activity using photocells.
2. **Give two CNS stimulants.** Caffeine and amphetamine.
3. **Give two CNS depressants.** Diazepam and chlorpromazine.
4. **Mechanism of caffeine?** Adenosine receptor blockade (and phosphodiesterase inhibition).
5. **Why should the arena be cleaned between animals?** The smell left by one animal changes the behaviour of the next.
practicals.title: Screening of CNS stimulants and depressants using an actophotometer

practicals.markdown:
# Anxiolytic activity using the elevated plus maze

**Aim:** To study the anxiolytic (anti-anxiety) activity of a drug such as diazepam in mice or rats using the elevated plus maze, by simulation.

## Principle

The elevated plus maze is a plus (+) shaped platform raised above the floor, with **two open arms** (no walls) and **two closed arms** (with high walls) meeting at a central square. Rodents naturally fear open and high spaces, so normally they spend more time in the **closed arms**. **Anxiolytic drugs** (benzodiazepines) reduce this fear, so animals make **more entries into the open arms and spend more time there**. Anxiogenic drugs have the opposite effect.

```text
                 Open arm
                    │
   Closed arm ──── centre ──── Closed arm      (raised above the floor)
                    │
                 Open arm
```

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: mice or rats, elevated plus maze, diazepam (standard), test drug, saline, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Divide the animals into control, standard and test groups and give saline, diazepam or test drug.
2. After the absorption time, place each animal in the central square facing an open arm.
3. For 5 minutes record:
   - number of entries into open arms and closed arms (all four paws in the arm);
   - time spent in open arms and closed arms.
4. Calculate the percentage of open-arm entries and time.

## Observations

| Group | Open-arm entries | Closed-arm entries | Time in open arms (s) | Time in closed arms (s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control | | | | |
| Diazepam | | | | |
| Test drug | | | | |

```text
 % open-arm entries = Open-arm entries ÷ (Open + Closed entries) × 100
 % time in open arms = Time in open arms ÷ (Time in open + closed arms) × 100
```

## Result

Diazepam increased the number of entries into and the time spent in the open arms, showing anxiolytic activity.

## Precautions

1. Test each animal only once (repeated testing changes behaviour).
2. Keep the room quiet with constant dim light.
3. Clean the maze between animals.
4. Use the same starting position for all animals.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the basis of the elevated plus maze?** Natural fear of open, raised spaces in rodents.
2. **What change do anxiolytics produce?** More open-arm entries and more time in open arms.
3. **Standard drug?** Diazepam.
4. **Mechanism of benzodiazepines?** Increase frequency of GABA-A chloride channel opening.
5. **Name a non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic.** Buspirone.
practicals.title: Anxiolytic activity using the elevated plus maze

practicals.markdown:
# Effect of drugs on the isolated frog heart

**Aim:** To study the effect of drugs (any two, for example adrenaline and acetylcholine, and the effect of atropine on acetylcholine) on the rate and force of contraction of the isolated frog heart, by simulation.

## Principle

A frog heart, perfused through a **Symes cannula** with oxygenated **frog Ringer solution**, keeps beating outside the body for hours. Its contractions are recorded on a kymograph or transducer. Drugs added to the perfusion fluid change the:

- **rate** (chronotropic effect) and
- **force/amplitude** (inotropic effect) of contraction.

| Drug | Receptor | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adrenaline | β1 | ↑ rate and ↑ force (positive chronotropic and inotropic) |
| Acetylcholine | M2 | ↓ rate and ↓ force; large dose may stop the heart in diastole |
| Atropine | Blocks M2 | Prevents the effect of acetylcholine |
| Propranolol | Blocks β1 | Prevents the effect of adrenaline |
| Digoxin | Na+/K+ ATPase | ↑ force; toxic doses – arrhythmia, systolic arrest |
| Calcium chloride (excess) | — | ↑ force |
| Potassium chloride (excess) | — | ↓ force and rate, diastolic arrest |

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: pithed frog, dissection set, Symes cannula, frog Ringer solution, heart lever, kymograph or recorder, drugs (adrenaline, acetylcholine, atropine), syringes.

## Procedure

1. In the simulation, the frog is pithed, the heart exposed and the Symes cannula tied into the sinus venosus/ventricle for perfusion with frog Ringer.
2. Attach the apex of the heart to the lever and record a **normal tracing** (baseline).
3. Add a dose of adrenaline into the perfusion; record the response; wash with Ringer until the tracing returns to normal.
4. Add acetylcholine and record; wash.
5. Add atropine, then acetylcholine again, and record (block of ACh effect).
6. Count heart rate (beats/min) and measure amplitude (mm) for each response.

## Observations

| Drug added | Heart rate (beats/min) | Amplitude (mm) | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Normal (Ringer) | | | Baseline |
| Adrenaline | | | |
| Acetylcholine | | | |
| Atropine + acetylcholine | | | |

```text
 % change in amplitude = (Amplitude after drug − Baseline amplitude) ÷ Baseline amplitude × 100
```

## Result

Adrenaline increased the rate and force of contraction; acetylcholine decreased both; atropine blocked the effect of acetylcholine.

## Precautions

1. Keep the heart moist and perfused with Ringer at a constant flow.
2. Avoid air bubbles in the cannula.
3. Wash the heart after each drug and wait for the baseline to return.
4. Add small doses first.

## Viva questions

1. **Name the cannula used.** Symes cannula.
2. **Composition of the perfusion fluid?** Frog Ringer solution (sodium chloride, potassium chloride, calcium chloride, sodium bicarbonate, glucose in water).
3. **Why does acetylcholine slow the heart?** It acts on M2 receptors and opens K+ channels (hyperpolarisation).
4. **What blocks adrenaline's effect on the heart?** β-blockers such as propranolol.
5. **What is a positive inotropic effect?** An increase in the force of contraction.
practicals.title: Effect of drugs on the isolated frog heart

practicals.markdown:
# Effect of drugs on ciliary motility of the frog buccal cavity

**Aim:** To study the effect of drugs on the ciliary movement of the frog's buccal (palate and oesophageal) mucosa, by simulation.

## Principle

The mucosa of the frog's mouth, palate and oesophagus is lined with **ciliated epithelium**. The cilia beat in one direction and carry particles towards the stomach. The **speed of ciliary movement** is measured by timing how long a small particle (such as a poppy seed or a bit of cork or charcoal) takes to travel a fixed distance.

- **Cholinergic drugs** (acetylcholine, pilocarpine, physostigmine) **increase** ciliary movement → particle moves faster (shorter time).
- **Anticholinergics** (atropine) and **local anaesthetics** (lidocaine) **decrease** it → longer time.

This relates to the clearance of mucus in human airways.

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: pithed frog, dissection board, pins, frog Ringer solution, poppy seeds, scale, stopwatch, drugs (acetylcholine or pilocarpine, atropine, lidocaine).

## Procedure

1. In the simulation, the pithed frog is pinned on its back; the lower jaw is cut and the buccal cavity and oesophagus are exposed and kept moist with Ringer.
2. Mark two points a fixed distance apart (e.g. 1 cm) on the palate.
3. Place a poppy seed at the upper mark and record the time taken to reach the lower mark. Repeat to get a steady **control time**.
4. Apply a few drops of the drug (e.g. acetylcholine) and after a minute repeat the timing.
5. Wash with Ringer, wait for recovery, then test the next drug (atropine, lidocaine).

## Observations

| Drug | Time to travel 1 cm (s), readings 1–3 | Mean time (s) | Speed (cm/s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ringer (control) | | | |
| Acetylcholine | | | |
| Atropine | | | |
| Lidocaine | | | |

```text
 Speed of ciliary movement = Distance ÷ Time
 % change = (Speed after drug − Control speed) ÷ Control speed × 100
```

## Result

Acetylcholine increased the speed of ciliary movement, while atropine and lidocaine decreased it.

## Precautions

1. Keep the mucosa moist with Ringer throughout.
2. Use particles of the same size and place them at the same mark.
3. Wash between drugs and wait for control values to return.

## Viva questions

1. **Which epithelium lines the frog buccal cavity?** Ciliated epithelium.
2. **Effect of acetylcholine on ciliary movement?** Increases it.
3. **Effect of atropine?** Decreases it (anticholinergic).
4. **Why is this experiment relevant to humans?** Airway cilia clear mucus; anticholinergics and some drugs can slow this clearance.
5. **What particle is used?** A poppy seed (or small cork or charcoal particle).
practicals.title: Effect of drugs on ciliary motility of the frog buccal cavity

practicals.markdown:
# Pyrogen testing by the rabbit method

**Aim:** To study the official rabbit pyrogen test for parenteral preparations, by simulation.

## Principle

**Pyrogens** are fever-producing substances, mainly **bacterial endotoxins** (lipopolysaccharides from the cell walls of gram-negative bacteria). They may be present in water for injection or injections even after sterilisation, because heat-stable endotoxins are not destroyed by autoclaving. When injected, they cause **fever, chills** and even shock. The pharmacopoeial **rabbit test** measures the **rise in body temperature** of rabbits after IV injection of the test solution. Rabbits are used because their temperature response to pyrogens resembles that of humans. The **bacterial endotoxin test (LAL test)**, using *Limulus* amoebocyte lysate, is an in vitro alternative that is now widely used.

## Requirements

Simulation software; in the simulated set-up: healthy adult rabbits of similar weight (kept in standard conditions and on the same diet), rabbit holders, clinical thermometer or electronic rectal probes, pyrogen-free (depyrogenated) syringes and needles (glassware heated, e.g. at 250 °C for at least 30 minutes), test solution warmed to about 37 °C.

## Procedure

1. Use healthy rabbits that have not been used for a pyrogen test recently and that have been trained to the holders; withhold food overnight before the test (water allowed).
2. Insert the thermometer or probe into the rectum to the fixed depth given in the pharmacopoeia; record temperatures at intervals before injection to get the **control (initial) temperature** of each rabbit.
3. Inject the test solution (usually 10 ml per kg body weight, or the dose in the monograph) slowly into the **marginal ear vein** within about 30 minutes of the control reading.
4. Record the temperature at regular intervals (e.g. every 30 minutes) for 3 hours after injection.
5. The **response** of each rabbit = highest temperature after injection − its control temperature (a fall is taken as zero).
6. Judge the result against the limits in the current pharmacopoeia.

## Observations

| Rabbit | Weight (kg) | Volume injected (ml) | Control temp (°C) | Max temp after injection (°C) | Rise (°C) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | | | | | |
| 2 | | | | | |
| 3 | | | | | |

```text
 Volume to inject = 10 ml/kg × body weight (kg)
 Rise for each rabbit = Maximum temperature after injection − Control temperature
```

**Interpretation (commonly taught pharmacopoeial scheme; check the current IP for exact limits):** the test starts with 3 rabbits. If no rabbit shows a rise of 0.5 °C or more, the sample passes. If any rabbit shows such a rise, the test is continued with 5 more rabbits, and the sample passes only if the number of rabbits with a rise and the total of the rises stay within the pharmacopoeial limits.

## Result

The sample was found to be **pyrogen-free / not pyrogen-free** according to the pharmacopoeial limits.

## Precautions

1. All glassware, syringes and needles must be pyrogen-free.
2. Rabbits must be calm and restrained gently; excitement raises temperature.
3. Keep the room temperature constant and avoid noise.
4. Insert the probe to the same depth each time.
5. Warm the injection to about body temperature and inject slowly.

## Viva questions

1. **What are pyrogens?** Fever-producing substances, mainly bacterial endotoxins (lipopolysaccharides of gram-negative bacteria).
2. **Why are rabbits used?** Their fever response to pyrogens is similar to that of humans.
3. **Which vein is used for injection?** The marginal ear vein.
4. **How is glassware made pyrogen-free?** Dry heat at a high temperature (e.g. 250 °C for at least 30 minutes).
5. **What is the in vitro alternative?** The bacterial endotoxin test (LAL test).
6. **Does autoclaving destroy pyrogens?** No, endotoxins are heat-stable; they are removed by dry heat depyrogenation, distillation or ultrafiltration.
practicals.title: Pyrogen testing by the rabbit method

questions.answer:
1. Classification: (a) Local – topical (skin, eye, ear, nose), deeper tissues (intra-articular); (b) Systemic – enteral (oral, sublingual/buccal, rectal) and parenteral (IV, IM, SC, intradermal, inhalation, transdermal, intrathecal/epidural).
2. Oral – advantages: safe, cheap, convenient, painless, self-administration, no sterility needed.
3. Oral – disadvantages: slow onset; not usable in vomiting, unconscious or uncooperative patients; some drugs destroyed by acid or enzymes (penicillin G, insulin); first-pass metabolism (nitroglycerin); irritant drugs cause nausea; absorption varies with food; bad taste.
4. IV – advantages: fastest onset, 100% bioavailability, exact control of dose and blood level; large volumes and irritant drugs (diluted) can be given; useful in emergencies and unconscious patients.
5. IV – disadvantages: needs sterile preparation and skill; once injected cannot be recalled; risk of thrombophlebitis, infection, air embolism, fluid overload and severe reactions; costly and painful; only aqueous solutions.
questions.question: Classify the routes of drug administration. Write the advantages and disadvantages of the oral and intravenous routes.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: chemical alteration of a drug in the body, mainly in the liver, usually into more polar, water-soluble and less active compounds that are easily excreted.
2. Results: inactivation (most drugs), active metabolite (diazepam → oxazepam), activation of prodrug (levodopa → dopamine, enalapril → enalaprilat), toxic metabolite (paracetamol → NAPQI).
3. Phase I (non-synthetic): oxidation by cytochrome P450 (commonest; phenytoin, barbiturates), reduction (chloramphenicol), hydrolysis (procaine, succinylcholine by esterases).
4. Phase II (conjugation): glucuronidation (commonest – morphine, paracetamol), acetylation (isoniazid, sulphonamides), sulphation, glycine conjugation, methylation, glutathione conjugation – products usually inactive and water-soluble.
5. Factors: age (newborn – grey baby syndrome with chloramphenicol; elderly – slow), genetics (slow/fast acetylators, pseudocholinesterase deficiency), enzyme induction (rifampicin, phenytoin, smoking), enzyme inhibition (erythromycin, ketoconazole, cimetidine), liver disease, diet, sex, pregnancy.
questions.question: Define biotransformation. Describe Phase I and Phase II reactions with examples and the factors that influence drug metabolism.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: movement of a drug from the site of administration into the systemic circulation.
2. Mechanisms: passive diffusion (most drugs; down gradient, needs lipid solubility), filtration through aqueous pores (small water-soluble molecules), facilitated diffusion (carrier, no energy), active transport (carrier + energy, against gradient, saturable – levodopa, iron), pinocytosis (vitamin B12 with intrinsic factor).
3. Ionisation: only unionised drug crosses membranes; weak acids unionised in stomach, weak bases in intestine; but most absorption occurs in the small intestine due to its large area.
4. Drug factors: lipid solubility, particle size, pKa, molecular size, dosage form (solution > suspension > tablet), formulation.
5. Physiological factors: surface area, blood flow, gastric emptying and motility, pH, food, disease, first-pass metabolism.
6. Interactions: antacids, milk and iron reduce absorption of tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones.
questions.question: Define drug absorption. Explain the mechanisms of absorption and the factors affecting it.

questions.answer:
1. Receptor-mediated actions – most drugs combine with specific receptor proteins (adrenaline on adrenoceptors).
2. Enzyme inhibition – neostigmine (cholinesterase), aspirin (COX), captopril (ACE), allopurinol (xanthine oxidase).
3. Ion channels – lidocaine blocks Na+ channels; nifedipine blocks Ca2+ channels; minoxidil opens K+ channels.
4. Transporters – omeprazole (H+/K+ ATPase), digoxin (Na+/K+ ATPase), furosemide (Na+-K+-2Cl−), fluoxetine (5-HT reuptake).
5. Physical/chemical actions – antacids, osmotic diuretics, chelators (dimercaprol), activated charcoal.
6. Agonist: affinity + intrinsic activity, activates receptor (adrenaline).
7. Antagonist: affinity without intrinsic activity, blocks agonist (atropine at muscarinic receptors; competitive antagonism is overcome by more agonist).
8. Partial agonist: submaximal response even at full occupancy; can block a full agonist (buprenorphine, pindolol).
9. Receptor families: ligand-gated ion channels, G-protein-coupled, kinase-linked, nuclear receptors.
questions.question: Explain the general mechanisms of drug action. Define agonist, antagonist and partial agonist with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged; IV = 100%; F = AUC oral ÷ AUC IV × 100.
2. Factors: drug properties (solubility, particle size, ionisation), dosage form and formulation, first-pass metabolism (GTN, propranolol), destruction in gut (penicillin G, insulin), gastric emptying and food, disease of gut or liver, drug interactions (antacids with tetracyclines), enzyme induction/inhibition.
questions.question: Define bioavailability. Write the factors affecting it.

questions.answer:
1. Metabolism of a drug in the gut wall and liver before it reaches the systemic circulation after oral use, reducing its bioavailability.
2. Examples: glyceryl trinitrate, propranolol, morphine, lidocaine (cannot be given orally), verapamil.
3. Avoided by sublingual (GTN), transdermal (nitroglycerin patch), inhalation, rectal (partly) and parenteral routes, or by giving larger oral doses.
questions.question: What is first-pass metabolism? Give examples and how it can be avoided.

questions.answer:
1. Lipid solubility and ionisation.
2. Plasma protein binding – acidic drugs bind albumin; bound drug is inactive; displacement interactions (aspirin displaces warfarin).
3. Blood flow to tissues (brain, heart, liver, kidney first).
4. Tissue binding (tetracyclines in bone, chloroquine in liver and retina).
5. Barriers – blood–brain barrier (only lipid-soluble drugs), placental barrier.
6. Redistribution (thiopentone) and volume of distribution.
questions.question: Write the factors affecting drug distribution.

questions.answer:
1. Body weight and age (children, elderly).
2. Sex, pregnancy and lactation.
3. Genetic factors – acetylator status, G6PD deficiency.
4. Route of administration (magnesium sulphate – purgative orally, anticonvulsant IV).
5. Disease – liver and kidney failure.
6. Tolerance, tachyphylaxis, cumulation.
7. Drug interactions – synergism (sulfamethoxazole + trimethoprim), antagonism (naloxone with morphine).
8. Placebo effect, diet and environment.
questions.question: Write a note on factors modifying drug action.

questions.answer: Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug – absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body – its actions and mechanism of action.
questions.question: Define pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.

questions.answer: The time taken for the plasma concentration of a drug to fall to half its value; about 4–5 half-lives are needed to reach steady state or to eliminate a drug almost completely.
questions.question: What is the half-life of a drug?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: drugs that produce effects like acetylcholine by stimulating cholinergic receptors directly or by inhibiting cholinesterase.
2. Classification: A. Direct-acting – choline esters (acetylcholine, methacholine, carbachol, bethanechol); alkaloids (pilocarpine, muscarine, arecoline). B. Anticholinesterases – reversible (physostigmine, neostigmine, pyridostigmine, edrophonium, donepezil, rivastigmine); irreversible (organophosphates – malathion, parathion; carbamates – carbaryl).
3. Neostigmine: quaternary reversible anticholinesterase; also direct NM stimulant; does not enter brain.
4. Actions: muscarinic – bradycardia, ↑ secretions, ↑ gut and bladder motility, miosis; nicotinic – ↑ skeletal muscle contraction.
5. Uses: myasthenia gravis; reversal of non-depolarising neuromuscular block (with atropine); postoperative urinary retention and paralytic ileus.
6. Adverse effects: sweating, salivation, colic, diarrhoea, bradycardia, bronchospasm.
7. Contraindications: bronchial asthma, intestinal/urinary obstruction, peptic ulcer, heart block.
questions.question: Define and classify cholinergic drugs. Write the pharmacological actions and uses of neostigmine.

questions.answer:
1. Classification: natural alkaloids – atropine, hyoscine; semisynthetic – homatropine, ipratropium, tiotropium, hyoscine butylbromide; synthetic – mydriatics (tropicamide, cyclopentolate), antisecretory/antispasmodic (glycopyrrolate, dicyclomine, propantheline), bladder (oxybutynin, tolterodine), antiparkinsonian (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine).
2. Actions: heart – tachycardia; glands – ↓ saliva, sweat, bronchial and gastric secretions; smooth muscle – relaxes gut, bladder, bronchi; eye – mydriasis, cycloplegia, ↑ IOP; CNS – stimulation in high doses; skin – flushing, fever in children.
3. Uses: pre-anaesthetic medication; organophosphate and mushroom poisoning; sinus bradycardia and heart block (0.6 mg IV); fundus examination, refraction, iritis; intestinal and biliary colic; motion sickness (hyoscine); asthma/COPD (ipratropium); parkinsonism.
4. Adverse effects: dry mouth, blurred vision, photophobia, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, delirium; poisoning treated with physostigmine.
5. Contraindications: angle-closure glaucoma, enlarged prostate, paralytic ileus, tachyarrhythmias.
questions.question: Classify anticholinergic drugs. Describe the pharmacological actions, uses and contraindications of atropine.

questions.answer:
1. Classification: non-selective – propranolol, timolol, sotalol, nadolol; β1-selective (cardioselective) – atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, nebivolol; with α-blocking action – labetalol, carvedilol; with partial agonist activity – pindolol.
2. Actions: ↓ heart rate, force and cardiac output; slow AV conduction; ↓ renin release; ↓ BP; ↓ myocardial O2 demand; ↓ aqueous humour formation; bronchoconstriction (β2 block); ↓ tremor.
3. Uses: hypertension, angina, after myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, chronic heart failure (carvedilol, metoprolol, bisoprolol), glaucoma (timolol), thyrotoxicosis, migraine prophylaxis, essential tremor, performance anxiety.
4. Adverse effects: bradycardia, heart block, bronchospasm, cold extremities, fatigue, masking of hypoglycaemia, vivid dreams; rebound angina on sudden withdrawal.
5. Contraindications: bronchial asthma and COPD, bradycardia and AV block, acute heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, variant angina; caution in diabetes.
questions.question: Classify β-adrenergic blockers. Write their pharmacological actions, uses, adverse effects and contraindications.

questions.answer:
1. Classification: A. Non-selective COX inhibitors – salicylates (aspirin); propionic acid (ibuprofen, naproxen); acetic acid (diclofenac, indomethacin, ketorolac); fenamate (mefenamic acid); oxicams (piroxicam); pyrazolone (metamizol). B. Preferential COX-2 – nimesulide, meloxicam. C. Selective COX-2 – celecoxib, etoricoxib. D. Analgesic-antipyretics with poor anti-inflammatory action – paracetamol.
2. Mechanism: aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX → ↓ prostaglandins and thromboxane A2.
3. Actions: analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory (high dose), antiplatelet (low dose).
4. Uses: pain, fever, rheumatoid arthritis and rheumatic fever; low dose 75–150 mg daily to prevent MI and stroke.
5. Adverse effects: gastric irritation, peptic ulcer and bleeding; prolonged bleeding time; hypersensitivity and aspirin-induced asthma; Reye's syndrome in children with viral fever; salicylism (tinnitus, vertigo) at high doses.
6. Contraindications: peptic ulcer, bleeding disorders, aspirin-sensitive asthma, children with viral fever, late pregnancy.
questions.question: Classify NSAIDs. Describe the mechanism of action, uses and adverse effects of aspirin.

questions.answer:
1. Remove contaminated clothes, wash skin; gastric lavage if swallowed.
2. Maintain airway, give oxygen and ventilate if needed.
3. Atropine IV in repeated doses until atropinisation (dry secretions, rising pulse) – blocks muscarinic effects.
4. Pralidoxime (cholinesterase reactivator) early, before ageing of the enzyme – helps nicotinic effects.
5. Diazepam for convulsions; supportive care.
questions.question: Write the treatment of organophosphate poisoning.

questions.answer:
1. Esters: cocaine, procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine (metabolised by plasma pseudocholinesterase).
2. Amides: lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine, dibucaine (metabolised in liver).
